questions.stem: Which combination of features is typical of Australopithecus afarensis?
options: Knuckle-walking, a large brain, and an opposable big toe for climbing
Brachiation, a small brain, and very large cheek teeth with a sagittal crest
Bipedal walking, a small ape-sized brain, and long arms with curved fingers
Bipedal walking, a brain as large as ours, and short arms with straight fingers
questions.explanation: Fossils such as the partial skeleton known as Lucy show that A. afarensis walked upright, but it had a brain usually under 500 cm³ and long arms with curved fingers, suggesting it also climbed trees.

questions.stem: Fossil footprints about 3.6 million years old at Laetoli in Tanzania are usually linked to Australopithecus afarensis. What do they show?
options: Hominins had already begun to make stone tools by then
Hominins had already spread from Africa into Asia
Hominins of that age had a brain as large as ours
Hominins were walking upright on two legs by that time
questions.explanation: The footprints, preserved in volcanic ash, show an upright, two-legged gait with a big toe in line with the others. This is direct evidence that bipedalism evolved long before large brains or stone tools appeared.

questions.stem: Approximately when did Australopithecus afarensis live?
options: About 400,000 to 40,000 years ago
About 300,000 years ago to the present
About 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago
About 1.8 to 1.2 million years ago
questions.explanation: A. afarensis is known from East African sites dated from roughly 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago. The later ranges listed belong to Paranthropus robustus, Neanderthals and Homo sapiens.

questions.stem: How does Australopithecus africanus compare with A. afarensis?
options: A rounder cranium, a larger brain and smaller teeth
A lower cranium, a smaller brain and much larger canines
A sagittal crest, a smaller brain and enormous cheek teeth
A modern skull shape, a brain the size of ours and a chin
questions.explanation: A. africanus, from southern Africa about 3.3 to 2.1 million years ago, had a rounder braincase housing a somewhat larger brain, and smaller teeth than A. afarensis, though its face was still prognathic.

questions.stem: The Taung child, found in South Africa in 1924, was the first early hominin skull found in Africa. To which species does it belong?
options: Paranthropus robustus
Homo neanderthalensis
Australopithecus africanus
Australopithecus afarensis
questions.explanation: The Taung child is a young individual of Australopithecus africanus. Its forward-placed foramen magnum suggested upright walking, an important early clue to hominin bipedalism.

questions.stem: Paranthropus robustus had very large cheek teeth, wide flaring cheekbones and a sagittal crest. What do these features suggest about its diet?
options: It chewed tough plant foods, needing powerful jaw muscles
It ate mainly soft meat, which it cut with large, sharp canines
It cooked all its food, so it needed only weak chewing muscles
It ate only fruit, which it swallowed without chewing at all
questions.explanation: The huge molars and the crest anchoring large jaw muscles indicate heavy chewing of tough plant material. The term robust refers to the skull and teeth, not to a large body.

questions.stem: Paranthropus robustus lived in southern Africa about 1.8 to 1.2 million years ago, at the same time as early Homo. How is it usually placed on hominin phylogenetic trees?
options: As the common ancestor of all the australopithecines
As a side branch that became extinct without giving rise to Homo
As the direct ancestor of Homo habilis and all later Homo species
As a descendant of Homo erectus that adapted to plant foods
questions.explanation: Its specialised chewing features and its existence alongside early Homo suggest Paranthropus was a separate lineage that died out. Exact relationships among hominins are debated, but it is not considered an ancestor of Homo.

questions.stem: Which feature of the australopithecines shows they were hominins rather than apes?
options: Their faces were completely flat, with no prognathism at all
Their stone tools were found alongside their earliest fossils
Their pelvis and leg bones show adaptations for bipedalism
Their brains were far larger than those of living great apes
questions.explanation: Australopithecines had ape-sized brains and prognathic faces, but their pelvis, femur and foot show upright walking, the key hominin feature. No stone tools have been found with A. africanus fossils.

questions.stem: Homo habilis means 'handy man'. Why was it given this name?
options: It was thought to be the first maker of stone tools
It was the first hominin found with a fully human hand
It was the first species to use fire for cooking
It was the first species to make clothing and needles
questions.explanation: H. habilis, found at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, was named because it was thought to have made the simple stone tools found at the same sites. Scientists still debate exactly which species made the earliest tools.

questions.stem: Compared with the australopithecines, how did Homo habilis differ?
options: A larger braincase and smaller teeth, though it kept fairly long arms
A smaller braincase and larger teeth, with a prominent sagittal crest
A fully modern skeleton, with a brain the same size as modern humans
A body built for brachiation, with arms twice as long as its legs
questions.explanation: H. habilis (about 2.4 to 1.4 million years ago) had a somewhat larger brain and smaller teeth than Australopithecus, but its long arms suggest it still climbed. Its face was moderately prognathic.

questions.stem: Which statement about Homo erectus is supported by fossil evidence?
options: It had a brain smaller than that of Australopithecus afarensis
It had human-like body proportions, with long legs and shorter arms
It had very long arms and curved fingers adapted to life in trees
It lived only in southern Africa and never spread to other continents
questions.explanation: H. erectus had long legs and relatively short arms, showing the loss of earlier climbing adaptations and an ability to walk long distances. Its fossils are found in Africa and across Asia, from Georgia to China and Indonesia.

questions.stem: Approximately when did Homo erectus live?
options: About 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago
About 400,000 to 40,000 years ago
About 300,000 years ago to the present
About 1.9 million to 110,000 years ago
questions.explanation: H. erectus was a long-lasting species, from roughly 1.9 million to about 110,000 years ago. Its range spread from Africa across much of Asia.

questions.stem: Homo erectus fossils have been found in Africa, Georgia, China and Indonesia. What does this distribution suggest?
options: Homo erectus could cross oceans only by building large boats
Hominins had spread from Africa across Asia by then
Homo erectus evolved separately in each of these four places
Asia was the original homeland of all hominins, not Africa
questions.explanation: Earlier hominins are known only from Africa, so finds of H. erectus in Asia show that hominins had dispersed beyond Africa. Its long legs and tool kit are thought to have helped it travel and live in varied environments.

questions.stem: Evidence for the controlled use of fire first appears within the time range of Homo erectus. How might fire have changed hominin lifestyles?
options: Fire allowed hominins to stop eating meat and rely entirely on raw plants
Fire increased the size of the teeth and jaws needed to chew cooked food
Fire was used mainly to make stone tools harder before they were struck
Cooking eased chewing and digestion; fire gave warmth and safety
questions.explanation: Cooking softens food and makes nutrients easier to absorb, which may have supported larger brains and smaller teeth. Fire also provided warmth, light and protection from predators.

questions.stem: Where and approximately when did Homo neanderthalensis live?
options: Southern Africa only, from about 3.3 to 2.1 million years ago
East Africa only, about 2.4 to 1.4 million years ago
Every continent, from about 300,000 years ago to the present
Europe and parts of Asia, about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago
questions.explanation: Neanderthal fossils come from Europe and south-western to central Asia, dated from roughly 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. The other ranges fit A. africanus, H. habilis and H. sapiens.

questions.stem: Which features describe a Neanderthal skull and body?
options: A high vertical forehead, small brow ridges, a chin and a tall, slender body
A sagittal crest, huge cheek teeth and a dish-shaped face on a small body
A small ape-sized brain, a projecting jaw and long arms with curved fingers
Large brow ridges, receding forehead, big nose and stocky body
questions.explanation: Neanderthals had a long, low skull with large brow ridges, a receding forehead and no chin, a large mid-face and nose, and a short, stocky build. A high vertical forehead and chin are modern human features.

questions.stem: Neanderthals had a short, stocky body with short lower limbs. How is this usually interpreted?
options: As evidence that they had smaller brains than us
As a way of conserving body heat in the cold
As an adaptation for swinging through forest trees
As evidence that they could not walk on two legs
questions.explanation: A compact body has less surface area relative to volume, which conserves heat, fitting the cold conditions of ice-age Europe. Neanderthals were fully bipedal and had brains as large as or larger than ours.

questions.stem: How did Neanderthal brain size compare with that of modern humans?
options: About half the size of ours
Slightly larger than a chimpanzee's
Similar to ours, often slightly larger
About one-third the size of a modern brain
questions.explanation: Neanderthal brains were as large as, and often larger than, modern human brains, in proportion to their heavier bodies. Brain shape differed, with a long, low braincase.

questions.stem: Which skull features are characteristic of Homo sapiens?
options: A small cranium, a projecting face, large canines and a diastema
A high rounded cranium, vertical forehead, small brow ridges, chin
A long, low cranium, a receding forehead, large brow ridges and no chin
A small cranium, a sagittal crest, wide cheekbones and huge molars
questions.explanation: Modern humans have a thin-walled, high-vaulted skull with a near-vertical forehead, little or no brow ridge, a flat face, small teeth and a projecting chin. Average brain size is about 1300 cm³.

questions.stem: Homo sapiens fossils about 300,000 years old have been found in Africa. Which conclusion is best supported by the fossil and genetic evidence?
options: Modern humans evolved in Africa and later spread to other continents
Modern humans evolved in Europe from Neanderthals and moved to Africa
Modern humans evolved separately on each continent from local apes
Modern humans evolved in Asia from Paranthropus about 300,000 years ago
questions.explanation: The oldest H. sapiens fossils are African, and genetic diversity is greatest in African populations, both supporting an African origin followed by dispersal. Some interbreeding with Neanderthals occurred after modern humans left Africa.

questions.stem: Which sequence lists these species from earliest to latest first appearance?
options: A. afarensis, H. erectus, H. habilis, H. neanderthalensis, H. sapiens
A. afarensis, H. habilis, H. neanderthalensis, H. erectus, H. sapiens
A. afarensis, H. habilis, H. erectus, H. neanderthalensis, H. sapiens
H. habilis, A. afarensis, H. erectus, H. sapiens, H. neanderthalensis
questions.explanation: Approximate first appearances: A. afarensis about 3.9 million years ago, H. habilis about 2.4 million, H. erectus about 1.9 million, Neanderthals about 400,000 and H. sapiens about 300,000 years ago.

questions.stem: Homo habilis and Homo erectus overlapped in time in East Africa. What does this suggest about drawing human evolution as a single straight line?
options: It is accurate, because no two hominin species ever lived together
It is misleading, because H. erectus evolved before H. habilis
It is misleading, as several species often lived at once
It is accurate, because each species changed directly into the next
questions.explanation: Fossils show that several hominin species, including Paranthropus, H. habilis and H. erectus, existed at the same time. Human evolution is better shown as a branching tree, with many lineages becoming extinct.

questions.stem: Across the hominin species studied, which overall trend is seen from Australopithecus to Homo sapiens?
options: Shorter legs, more curved fingers and less tool use
Larger brains, flatter faces and smaller teeth
Smaller brains, longer arms and larger canines
Larger teeth, a higher crest and a smaller brain
questions.explanation: Over time, brain size increased, the face became less prognathic and the teeth and jaws became smaller, while tool use became more complex. Arms became relatively shorter as climbing adaptations were lost.

questions.stem: A fossil skull has a brain volume of about 1000 cm³, large brow ridges, a long low cranium and no chin, and is about 1 million years old. Which species does it most likely belong to?
options: Paranthropus robustus
Homo erectus
Homo sapiens
Australopithecus afarensis
questions.explanation: A brain much larger than an australopithecine's but smaller than ours, with large brow ridges, a long low cranium and no chin, fits H. erectus, which lived at that time. H. sapiens appeared only about 300,000 years ago.

questions.stem: Which tool culture is associated with Homo habilis?
options: Oldowan
Acheulean
Mousterian
Upper Palaeolithic
questions.explanation: The Oldowan, named after Olduvai Gorge, is the earliest known stone tool culture, dating from at least 2.6 million years ago, and is linked with early Homo such as H. habilis. The Acheulean is associated with H. erectus.

questions.stem: How were Oldowan tools made?
options: A hammerstone knocked sharp flakes off a core, with little shaping
A core was carefully shaped on both faces into a symmetrical teardrop
A core was prepared so a flake of planned shape came off in one blow
Long thin blades were punched from a core and fitted to wooden handles
questions.explanation: Oldowan toolmakers struck cobbles with a hammerstone to produce sharp flakes and simple choppers. The flakes were used to cut meat and plants. Two-faced teardrop handaxes are Acheulean.

questions.stem: Which tool culture is associated with Homo erectus?
options: Mousterian
Aurignacian
Acheulean
Oldowan
questions.explanation: The Acheulean, beginning about 1.76 million years ago, is associated with H. erectus. Its characteristic tool is the large, two-faced handaxe.

questions.stem: What is the characteristic tool of the Acheulean culture?
options: A thin needle made of bone with an eye
A small blade fitted into an arrow shaft
A symmetrical, two-faced handaxe
A simple sharp flake struck from a pebble
questions.explanation: Acheulean handaxes are flaked on both sides (bifacial) into a regular teardrop or oval shape, with long cutting edges. They were made in much the same form for over a million years.

questions.stem: Why do archaeologists infer that the makers of Acheulean handaxes had greater cognitive abilities than the makers of Oldowan tools?
options: They needed a planned shape kept in mind through many strikes
Handaxes were made from bone, which needs more skill than stone to work
Handaxes were found with written records explaining how they were made
Handaxes were produced by a single blow, which needed great accuracy
questions.explanation: Making a symmetrical handaxe requires imagining the finished form and removing flakes in a planned sequence to achieve it. Oldowan flakes needed far less planning.

questions.stem: Which tool culture is associated with Homo neanderthalensis?
options: Oldowan
Acheulean
Aurignacian
Mousterian
questions.explanation: Neanderthals made Mousterian tools, sophisticated flake tools detached from prepared stone cores. Oldowan and Acheulean tools are older cultures, and the Aurignacian is an early Upper Palaeolithic culture of H. sapiens.

questions.stem: What was the key advance in Mousterian toolmaking?
options: Casting metal into moulds to make blades with sharper edges
Preparing a core so a flake of planned shape could be struck off
Using a hammerstone to strike any sharp flake off a river pebble
Grinding stone into polished axes for clearing land to farm
questions.explanation: Mousterian toolmakers shaped a core in advance (the prepared-core or Levallois technique) so that one blow produced a flake of a predetermined size and shape. These flakes were made into scrapers and points.

questions.stem: Neanderthals made stone points and thrusting spears, and made clothing from animal hides. What do these show about their lifestyle?
options: They hunted large animals and coped with cold climates
They lived only in warm forests and ate mainly fruit and leaves
They farmed crops and kept domesticated animals in villages
They scavenged only, as they could not make tools for hunting
questions.explanation: Spears and stone points indicate hunting, and scrapers were used to prepare hides, which supports clothing for cold ice-age climates. Farming came much later, with Homo sapiens.

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of the Upper Palaeolithic tool cultures made by Homo sapiens?
options: Large teardrop handaxes made in the same form for a million years
Prepared-core flakes used as scrapers with no other materials
Long, thin stone blades and tools of bone, antler and ivory
Simple sharp flakes struck from river pebbles with a hammerstone
questions.explanation: Upper Palaeolithic toolmakers struck long, narrow blades from prepared cores and also worked bone, antler and ivory into items such as needles, harpoons and spear throwers.

questions.stem: Making long blades from a prepared core gives far more cutting edge from a given amount of stone than earlier methods. Why might this have mattered to Homo sapiens?
options: Blades were heavier than handaxes, so they stayed sharp for much longer
Blades needed no planning, so even very young children could make them
Stone was used efficiently, so people could live far from good sources
Blades could be made without a hammer, so no other tools were needed at all
questions.explanation: Efficient use of stone meant people carried less raw material and could live in areas where good stone was scarce. Blade production involved careful planning, reflecting advanced cognition.

questions.stem: Sewing needles made of bone, fishhooks, harpoons and spear throwers are found at Homo sapiens sites. What do these tools suggest?
options: General-purpose tools used for every task in exactly the same way
Tools made only from stone, as other materials were never used
Tools that were made by Homo erectus and later reused by H. sapiens
Specialised tools for tasks such as making clothes and fishing
questions.explanation: These items show a wide range of specialised tools made from varied materials, allowing people to tailor clothing, fish and hunt from a distance. They indicate complex planning and diverse lifestyles.

questions.stem: Which overall trend is seen from Oldowan to Upper Palaeolithic tool cultures?
options: Simpler tools made only from stone, produced in fewer stages over time
Larger, heavier tools with less cutting edge from the same amount of stone
Identical tools in every culture, showing that cognitive ability did not change
More complex, specialised tools made from a wider range of materials
questions.explanation: Tools became more refined and varied, with more planning, more standardised forms, more specialised uses and the use of bone, antler and other materials. This is taken as evidence of increasing cognitive abilities.

questions.stem: Stone tools found with fossils are used as evidence of hominin cognition. Which is a limitation of this evidence?
options: Stone tools were made only by modern humans, so they tell us nothing of others
Stone tools always occur with the bones of the species that made them
Wooden and other perishable tools rarely survive, biasing the record
Stone tools cannot be dated, so they give no information about time
questions.explanation: Perishable tools usually decay, so the surviving record is biased towards stone. It can also be hard to know which species made a tool, since tools are not always found with fossils and several species may have lived nearby.
